segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Welcome back. Today we are on measuring the macroeconomy: how we measure a whole economy with numbers. In the early 1930s, during the Great Depression, American leaders could not say how bad the crisis was. Why not?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Because nobody had measured the whole economy yet. They had only stock prices and a few counts of factory output. So the economist Simon Kuznets and a team at the U.S. Department of Commerce built the national accounts: records that add up a country's production, spending and income.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the best-known number in those accounts is GDP?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. GDP is short for gross domestic product. It's the value of all the final goods and services a country produces in a year, counted at the prices people pay. Final means that a good has reached its last user, like the bread you eat, not the flour inside it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So when GDP grows, the country makes more goods?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Not only that. Prices matter too. Here's a modern puzzle. From 1995 to 2022, U.S. GDP measured in dollars became about 3.4 times as large. But the amount of goods and services produced did not even double. The rest came from higher prices.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So here is today's question. How do we count a whole economy, and split its growth into higher prices and more goods?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: By the end of this episode, you'll be able to do three things. First, say who buys and who earns U.S. GDP, and explain why production, spending and income are three ways to count the same total. Second, split the growth of GDP in dollars into higher prices and more goods, and explain why the choice of prices matters. Third, explain why we compare countries at common prices, the same prices for every country, and name what GDP leaves out.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And we'll follow the chapter's mind map part by part?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. Part one gives the facts. Part two builds the accounting framework behind them. Part three shows the uses and limits of GDP. Each part has three or four leaves, small topics that we take in order.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Part one of the map: The facts. The first leaf asks who buys GDP. So who does buy it?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Economists split the buyers into four groups. Households buy consumption goods and services, like food, rent and medical care. Firms buy investment goods: new buildings, machines and software. The government buys goods and services, like the work of teachers and new roads. And people in other countries buy the country's exports.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And what about the things we buy from other countries?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Those are imports. We subtract them, because they were made somewhere else. Exports minus imports are called net exports.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Which group is the biggest? Firms and the government spend huge amounts. My guess is that households buy about half.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Households buy even more than that, because consumption covers everything families buy, day after day. From 1950 to 2025, consumption averaged about 64 percent of U.S. GDP. That's close to two-thirds.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the shares hardly change at all?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: They change, but slowly. Since 1970, consumption's share has risen by 7.4 percentage points. A percentage point is the simple difference between two percentages. So out of every 100 dollars of GDP, consumers now buy 7.4 dollars more than they did then.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Then another share had to fall. I'd guess investment, because money spent in shops is not invested.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: It sounds logical, but investment actually ended a little higher. The government bought less, and the country bought more abroad than it sold. Government purchases lost 6.2 points, and net exports lost 3.4 points. The four shares always add up to 100 percent, so the points some shares gain, others must lose. Net exports are now negative, which is called a trade deficit.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: who earns GDP.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Every dollar of GDP is also someone's income. Part of it goes to workers as wages, salaries and benefits. Apart from some taxes, the rest goes to the owners of capital, meaning buildings, machines and other tools. Labor's share is the part of income that pays for work.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: I learned that workers always get about two-thirds of income. So my guess is that labor's share stays at two-thirds.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: You're half right. On average, it's close to two-thirds. But the share is not constant. In 1970 it was 0.69. That means workers earned 69 cents of every dollar of income.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And today?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: In 2025, it was 0.59, the lowest in the data. So labor's share has slowly fallen for more than five decades. In part three, we ask why.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: The last leaf of this part is prices. How much have prices gone up?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Here we follow the price level, the average price of everything counted in GDP. Guess first. How many times higher is the U.S. price level now than in 1947?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Hmm. Maybe five times higher?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: More than twice that, because small rises every year build on each other over almost eight decades. The price level is about 12 times its 1947 level. On average, what cost one dollar in 1947 costs about 12 dollars now. The growth rate of the price level is called inflation. It's the percent by which prices go up in a year.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So when was inflation highest?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: In the 1970s. It peaked at 10.9 percent in 1975.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And has high inflation come back since then?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. A second wave peaked at 7.8 percent in 2022.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So in part one we saw three facts. Households buy most of what the U.S. economy produces. Workers earn most of its income, but a smaller part than in 1970. And prices keep going up, but not at a steady pace.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Right. But every one of these facts depends on definitions. Next branch: how the accounts are built, and why their numbers fit together.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Part two of the map: The accounting framework. The first leaf says production equals expenditure equals income. What does that mean?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Expenditure simply means spending. We can count GDP by adding up what is produced, what is spent on it, or the incomes it pays. All three give the same total. Let's see why on Islandia, a small imaginary island country that we come back to often.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: My guess is that they just add up every sale on the island.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: That would count some things more than once. A farm sells grain worth 40 dollars to a mill. The mill makes flour and sells it for 70 dollars to a bakery. The bakery sells bread worth 120 dollars to islanders.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So all the sales add up to 230 dollars.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes, but the grain is inside the flour, and the flour is inside the bread. So 230 counts the grain three times and the flour twice. The answer is value added: what a firm sells, minus what it buys from other firms. For the mill, that's 70 dollars of flour minus 40 dollars of grain, so 30 dollars.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the farm adds 40, because it buys nothing from other firms. And the bakery adds 120 minus 70, which is 50.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Exactly. Add the three, and you get 120 dollars, the value of the bread. Each dollar of value added is also someone's income. It pays workers, taxes, and machines that wear out, called depreciation. Profit is whatever is left for the owners, so the incomes also add up to 120 dollars.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: who buys it. We met those buyers in part one.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Now they become a rule. GDP equals consumption plus investment plus government purchases plus net exports. This is the national income identity. An identity is true by definition, in every year and every country.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But what if a firm can't sell what it makes?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Suppose Harbor Boatworks, a boat builder on Islandia, can't sell a boat this year. The boat counts as investment in inventories, meaning goods made but not yet sold. It's as if the boat builder had bought its own boat. So every good produced has a buyer somewhere in the accounts.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Here's something I've always believed. Imports come with a minus sign. So when islanders buy more imports, GDP falls.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: A lot of students think that, but imports don't lower GDP directly. Suppose an islander buys a new boat built on Mainland, the country that Islandia trades with. Consumption goes up by the price of the boat, and so do imports, so net exports fall by the same amount. The two changes cancel. The minus sign only removes goods made abroad, which were already counted in spending. GDP falls only if the islander would otherwise have bought a boat from Harbor Boatworks, and that's a question about behavior.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: real GDP holds prices fixed. Why do we need to keep prices the same?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: GDP in dollars, called nominal GDP, can grow because goods cost more or because there are more goods. Real GDP values each year's goods at the same prices, so it changes only when quantities change. Back to Islandia. In this example, it makes only apples and computers.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Does it matter which prices? Growth is growth, I'd say.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: You'd think so, but the answer changes a little. Let's build the answer at the old prices step by step. In 2026, Islandia spends 6,000 dollars in all: 5,000 on computers and 1,000 on apples.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And what happens the next year?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: In 2027, Islandia makes 10 percent more apples and 20 percent more computers. To measure real growth, we value these extra goods at the old 2026 prices.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the extra apples are worth 10 percent of 1,000 dollars. That's 100 dollars.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Right. And the extra computers are worth 20 percent of 5,000 dollars, which is 1,000 dollars. Together, the extra goods are worth 1,100 dollars.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And we started from 6,000. So real growth is 1,100 divided by 6,000?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes, about 18.3 percent. So real growth is an average of the two growth rates. Computers count much more in that average, because they had five sixths of the spending. This measure is called the Laspeyres index: growth at the starting prices.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And at 2027 prices?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: In 2027, an apple costs 3 dollars instead of 2, but a computer costs the same as before. So computers became cheaper compared with apples, and they take a smaller share of spending. The fast-growing good counts for less in the average, so real growth comes out lower, at 17.7 percent. Growth at the ending prices is called the Paasche index.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Two answers for the same island. Which one is right?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Neither is wrong. Each one uses a different year's prices. Statistical offices take the average of the two, which here is 18.0 percent. Over many years, one set of prices goes out of date. So offices use the prices of two neighboring years at a time, and link the years like a chain. That's called chain weighting. The United States moved to it in the 1990s, when computer prices were falling fast.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Last leaf of this part: prices link the two measures, GDP in dollars and real GDP.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: GDP in dollars equals the price level times real GDP. So GDP in dollars grows for two reasons, higher prices and more goods. Take 2022. Prices went up 7.1 percent, and real GDP grew 2.4 percent.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So GDP in dollars grew by the sum, about 9.5 percent?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Very close: it grew 9.7 percent. Adding leaves out one small piece, the price rise on the extra goods. When both changes are small, that piece is tiny. So the growth of GDP in dollars is about inflation plus real growth.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Now the modern puzzle from the opening. GDP in dollars became about 3.4 times as large. How much was more goods?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Real GDP became 1.93 times as large, so output almost doubled. Over those 27 years, prices went up by about three quarters.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So can we add the two growth rates, like in 2022?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Not here. Both changes are big, so the price rise on all the extra goods is big too. Instead, we multiply. The price level became 1.76 times as high, and 1.76 times 1.93 is about 3.4.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So in part two we saw that value added counts each stage once, and that spending and income add up to the same total. Real GDP keeps prices the same, but the prices we pick change the answer a little.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. Next branch: we use these tools to compare countries, and we look at what GDP misses.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Part three of the map: Uses and limits. The first leaf: compare at common prices. Why is it hard to compare countries?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Because countries use different currencies, like Islandia and Mainland. The simple way is to convert with the exchange rate, the price of one currency in another. Take China and the United States in 2019. Converted at the exchange rate, China's GDP was 67 percent of U.S. GDP.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: A dollar is a dollar. So that comparison sounds fair to me.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: It sounds fair, but it misses one thing: prices differ between countries. In 2019, goods in China cost almost a third less than the same goods in the United States. So each dollar of China's GDP stands for more goods.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So how do we correct for that?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: We value China's goods at U.S. prices. To do that, we divide China's GDP in dollars by China's prices as a share of U.S. prices. That share is below one, so China's GDP gets larger. At common prices, China's economy was 98 percent of the U.S. economy, almost the same size. This is called purchasing power parity, or PPP: comparing countries at the same prices.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So China was almost as rich as the United States?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: No. That's the whole economy. China has about 4 times as many people, so per person it was still only about a quarter of the U.S. level.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But why are goods cheaper in China?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Services like haircuts can't be shipped, and they need a lot of work, so they are cheap where wages are low. Suppose a haircut on Islandia costs half as much as on Mainland. At the exchange rate, it counts as half a Mainland haircut, though it's the same service. So exchange rates make poorer countries look poorer than they are.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: beyond GDP. What does GDP leave out?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: GDP counts mostly what is sold in markets. If you cook dinner at home, only the groceries count, not your time. A restaurant meal counts in full. GDP also leaves out how long and how healthy people's lives are, how much free time they have, and damage to the environment.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Then GDP must be a poor guide to how well people live.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: You're partly right: for one country, it can miss a lot. Two economists at Stanford built a broader measure of welfare, meaning how good people's lives are. It starts from what people consume, and adds the value of longer lives, more free time and a fairer sharing of consumption. In 2007, France's GDP per person was about 70 percent of the U.S. level.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And with the broader measure?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: French people lived longer, worked fewer hours, and shared consumption more equally. So France's welfare was about 91 percent of the U.S. level. But across more than 100 countries, welfare and GDP were very closely linked. Countries with higher GDP usually had higher welfare too. So GDP is imperfect, but it's not a poor guide.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: who gains from growth? Back to labor's falling share. Why did it fall?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Economists still debate it. One idea is that cheaper machines and software replace some workers. Another is that a few very large firms with few workers have taken a bigger part of their markets. A third is that workers have less power to ask for higher pay, because of global trade and weaker unions. And part of the fall comes from how statisticians count software and research, which is also debated.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Does it matter which explanation is right?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes, for policy. If machines replace workers, it points to training, and to how we tax capital and labor. If big firms are the cause, it points to competition policy, meaning rules that stop firms from gaining too much power over a market. If workers lost power, it points to the rules of the labor market. And if it's only a question of counting, no response is needed.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Last leaf: check the definitions before comparing.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: The World Bank counts government spending on roads, buildings and equipment as investment. The Bureau of Economic Analysis, which builds the U.S. accounts, counts it as government purchases. So for the United States, the World Bank's investment share is about 4 points higher, and its government share about 4 points lower.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So it's the same spending, just put in a different group.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Exactly. So before you compare two countries, check that the numbers use the same definitions.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So in part three we saw that countries must be compared at the same prices, that GDP leaves out a lot, and that who gains from growth is still debated.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Right. Let's sum up.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's go back to our three goals. First, who buys and who earns GDP, and why are production, spending and income the same total?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Households buy about two-thirds of U.S. GDP, and workers earn most of the income, though a falling share. The three counts agree because value added counts each stage once, and every dollar of value added is someone's income.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Second, splitting growth. Real GDP holds prices fixed, so it shows only the goods.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. But the prices you choose change the answer a little, 18.3 or 17.7 percent, because computers grew fastest and got cheaper, so they count more at the old prices. So offices average the two answers and link the years in a chain.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And third, comparing countries.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Use common prices, because poorer countries usually have lower prices. And remember what GDP leaves out: health, free time, work at home and the environment.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So what's the one idea to keep?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Measure before you model. In the coming chapters, we build models, simple stories of how the economy works. But first we must measure it well. GDP is one total that we can count in three ways. Its growth splits into higher prices and more goods. And countries must be compared at the same prices.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Here's a question to think about. Suppose Islandia's currency loses value against Mainland's, so one unit of Islandia's money buys less of Mainland's money. Nothing else changes in either country. What happens to Islandia's GDP compared with Mainland's? First at the exchange rate, and then at common prices.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Pause the episode and think about it for a moment.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Okay, we're back. What's the answer?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: At the exchange rate, Islandia looks smaller. Its GDP is worth less in Mainland's money, by the same percent as its currency fell. At common prices, nothing changes. Islandia still makes the same goods, and its prices in Mainland's money fell by that same percent. At common prices, we divide its GDP in Mainland's money by its prices in Mainland's money. Both fell by the same percent, so the result does not move. That's why common prices are better for comparing what countries produce.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Where can students try all this themselves?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Open the chapter's Colab notebook to rebuild every chart and calculation yourself. And the Data Apps let you explore the charts without any code.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And next time?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: In Chapter 3, we use real GDP per person at common prices, the measure we built today. We ask: why are some countries so much richer than others, and how do we read growth from the data?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's it for today. Thanks for listening, and see you next time.
